title: Word frequency
statement:
Write `word_freq(text: str) -> dict[str, int]` that counts how often each word appears.
Words are case-insensitive and separated by whitespace; strip the punctuation `.,!?` from word edges.
expected: Returns a dict mapping lowercase words to counts. Empty or whitespace-only text returns `{}`.
hints: Normalize first: `.lower()` then `.split()`.
`str.strip('.,!?')` removes punctuation from both ends.
`collections.Counter` does the counting; convert to `dict`.
explanation: Lowercasing and splitting normalizes input; a generator strips punctuation lazily; `if w` drops tokens that were only punctuation. Counter is O(n).

title: Flatten nested lists
statement: Write `flatten(items)` that takes a list which may contain nested lists to any depth and returns a flat list of the non-list values, in order.
expected: Order is preserved. Empty nested lists contribute nothing.
hints: Recursion fits naturally: a list's flattening is the concatenation of its elements' flattenings.
Check `isinstance(x, list)`.
A generator with `yield from` avoids building intermediate lists.
explanation: `yield from` delegates to the recursive generator. Each element is visited once: O(n) over all values. Very deep nesting can hit Python's recursion limit; an explicit stack avoids that.

title: Retry decorator
statement: Write a decorator factory `retry(times: int, exceptions=(Exception,))` that re-calls the decorated function when it raises one of `exceptions`, up to `times` total attempts. If every attempt fails, re-raise the last exception. Preserve the function's name with `functools.wraps`.
expected: Successful calls return the function's value. Exceptions not listed in `exceptions` propagate immediately without retrying.
hints: You need three levels: `retry(...)` returns a decorator, which returns a wrapper.
Loop `for attempt in range(times)`; `return` on success.
Keep the last exception and `raise` it after the loop.
explanation: The factory captures configuration, the decorator captures the function, and the wrapper runs the attempts. Catching only `exceptions` means programming errors like KeyError aren't hidden by retries. In production, add a delay with exponential backoff and jitter between attempts.

title: Batch a stream
statement: Write a generator `chunked(iterable, size)` that yields lists of up to `size` items. It must work on any iterable, including generators that can only be consumed once, without loading everything into memory.
expected: The last chunk may be shorter. `size` must be a positive integer, otherwise raise `ValueError`.
hints: Use `iter()` so you can pull items in a loop.
`itertools.islice(it, size)` takes up to `size` items.
Stop when a chunk comes back empty.
explanation: Memory stays at O(size) because only one chunk exists at a time. This is the pattern for bulk-inserting millions of rows in batches. (Python 3.12 adds `itertools.batched`, which yields tuples.)

title: Valid brackets
statement: Write `is_balanced(s: str) -> bool` returning True if every `(`, `[` and `{` is closed by the matching bracket in the correct order. Other characters are ignored.
expected: Runs in O(n). An empty string is balanced.
hints: The most recently opened bracket must close first: that's a stack.
Push openers; on a closer, the stack top must be its partner.
At the end, the stack must be empty.
explanation: A stack models nesting: O(n) time, O(n) space in the worst case. The same idea powers parsers and expression evaluators.

title: Two sum
statement: Write `two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None` returning the indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` of two numbers adding to `target`, or `None` if none exist. Solve it in one pass.
expected: O(n) time. If several pairs exist, return the first completed while scanning left to right.
hints: For each number x, the partner you need is `target - x`.
Store numbers you've seen in a dict: value → index.
Check for the partner before inserting x (handles duplicates like [3, 3]).
explanation: Trading O(n) memory for O(n) time instead of the O(n²) brute force. Note `is not None`: index 0 is falsy, so `if i:` would be a bug.

title: Binary search
statement: Write `search(sorted_nums: list[int], target: int) -> int` returning the index of `target` in a sorted list, or `-1`. Do not use `list.index` or `bisect`.
expected: O(log n). Works for empty lists and single elements.
hints: Keep `lo` and `hi` bounds of the search range.
Compare with the middle element and discard half.
Loop while `lo <= hi`; watch for off-by-one errors.
explanation: Each iteration halves the range, so at most about log₂(n) + 1 comparisons. B-tree indexes in PostgreSQL apply the same idea across disk pages.

title: Paginate a list endpoint
statement:
Write `paginate(items: list, page: int, size: int) -> dict` for an API that returns `{"data": [...], "page": page, "size": size, "total": n, "next": next_page_or_None}`.
Validate input: `page` starts at 1; `size` must be 1–100. Invalid values raise `ValueError` (your view would turn it into a 400).
expected: A page past the end returns an empty `data` list and `next: None`.
hints: Offset = (page - 1) * size.
There is a next page if offset + size < total.
Validate before computing anything.
explanation: Capping `size` protects the server from `?size=1000000`. In a real database this becomes `LIMIT size OFFSET start`; for very large tables switch to cursor (keyset) pagination.

title: Fixed-window rate limiter
statement: Implement `RateLimiter(limit, window_seconds)` with `allow(client_id, now) -> bool`. Each client may make at most `limit` requests per fixed window (window number = `now // window_seconds`). `now` is passed in so the class is testable without sleeping.
expected: Clients are independent. A new window resets the count. Return False when the limit is exceeded (your API returns 429).
hints: Store `(window, count)` per client in a dict.
If the stored window differs from the current one, reset the count.
Injecting `now` makes time-based code deterministic in tests.
explanation: Fixed windows are simple but allow bursts at window edges (2× limit across a boundary); sliding-window or token-bucket algorithms smooth that. In production the counters live in Redis (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) so all app instances share them — this is what DRF throttling does with a cache backend.

title: Typed settings from the environment
statement:
Write `load_settings(env: dict) -> dict` that reads `DEBUG`, `PORT` and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` from a dict of strings (like `os.environ`):
- `DEBUG`: True only for `1`, `true`, `yes` (any case); default False.
- `PORT`: int, default 8000; raise `ValueError` if not an integer from 1 to 65535.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS`: comma-separated, whitespace trimmed, empty entries removed; default `[]`.
- `SECRET_KEY`: required; raise `KeyError` if missing.
expected: Never treat the string 'False' as truthy. Fail fast on missing required values.
hints: Write a small `parse_bool` helper.
`int()` raises ValueError for bad input; then check the range.
Use `env['SECRET_KEY']` (not `.get`) so a missing key raises.
explanation: Taking `env` as a parameter instead of reading `os.environ` directly makes the function pure and testable. Libraries like pydantic-settings and django-environ do this with type annotations.

title: Top customers by revenue
statement:
Tables: `customers(id, email)` and `orders(id, customer_id, total numeric, status text, created_at timestamptz)`.
Return the 3 customers with the highest total revenue from **paid** orders in 2024, as `email, orders, revenue`, highest revenue first.

examples.input: customers: ana, ben, chi; ana has 2 paid orders (10, 20), ben 1 paid (50) and 1 cancelled (100)

expected: Cancelled orders don't count. Customers with no paid orders in 2024 don't appear. Ties may be in any order.
hints: JOIN orders to customers.
Filter status and date range in WHERE — use a half-open range `>= '2024-01-01' AND < '2025-01-01'`.
GROUP BY the customer, aggregate with count and sum, ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3.
starter:
SELECT ...
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...

solution.code:
SELECT c.email,
       count(*)     AS orders,
       sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
  AND o.created_at <  '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.email
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;

explanation: An INNER JOIN is right here because customers without paid orders should be excluded. The half-open date range is index-friendly and avoids missing orders at 23:59:59.5 on Dec 31. Grouping by `c.id` (not just email) keeps distinct customers distinct. An index on `orders (status, created_at)` or `(customer_id)` helps at scale.

title: Customers who never ordered
statement: Using the same tables, list the emails of customers who have **never** placed an order, alphabetically.

examples.input: customers: ana (2 orders), ben (0 orders), chi (0 orders)

expected: Customers with any order (any status) are excluded.
hints: You need rows that have no match: an anti-join.
Option 1: `LEFT JOIN orders` then `WHERE o.id IS NULL`.
Option 2: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders ...)`.
explanation: `NOT EXISTS` states the intent directly and the planner runs it as an anti-join. Avoid `NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`: if any customer_id is NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all.
